title: Podcast with Stephen DiAdamo, Co-founder and CTO of Qoro Quantum - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Qoro Quantum, a two-year-old UK/Germany middleware startup, is building an orchestration layer (Divi SDK + Maestro simulator router) that abstracts quantum hardware away from applications, deliberately refusing to build its own transpilers, error correction, or hardware. Its sharpest commercial argument is not future scaling but present-day resilience: an all-day IBM outage that took down six machines at once is used as proof that HPC centers need multi-vendor, multi-modality QPU fallback today. The business is monetized as open-core plus pay-as-you-go cloud credits, with emulation-based HPC 'integration demos' priced at 100k-200k to displace million-dollar QPU purchases.

themes.theme: Middleware positioning and deliberate stack boundaries

insights.claim: Qoro Quantum positions itself as a middleware company that works top-down from applications into orchestration across CPUs, GPUs and QPUs of different modalities, rather than competing at the hardware or application layer.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Middleware is the least-crowded layer of the quantum stack; a winner here collects value regardless of which hardware modality wins, making it a hedge against modality risk.
insights.quote: you can consider us a software middleware company looking at simplifying infrastructure deployments and accessing many quantum computers from any vendor in a seamless and automated way
insights.locator: So I’m Stephen DiAdamo. I am the CTO

insights.claim: Qoro's stated goal is to remove the PhD requirement from quantum computing by turning applications into familiar parameter inputs, which reframes the addressable market from quantum specialists to ordinary domain engineers.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: If quantum access de-skills, the bottleneck shifts from scarce quantum PhDs to compute capacity — bullish for simulation/HPC vendors, bearish for consultancy-style quantum services.
insights.quote: PhD is not necessary to have anymore because the applications are inputs that people are familiar with
insights.locator: we do is make it as easy as possible to access

insights.claim: Qoro explicitly refuses to build transpilation techniques and relies entirely on each hardware vendor's own transpiler and compiler, only wrapping thin software around heuristic passes to improve them.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: This is a strategic moat decision: Qoro captures routing/automation value without carrying compiler R&D cost, but it also means its performance ceiling is set by vendor toolchains it does not control.
insights.quote: we don’t invent transpilation techniques. We always rely on the vendor to provide the transpilation methods
insights.locator: Yeah, so we don’t invent transpilation techniques

insights.claim: Cross-modality circuit compilation is acknowledged as an unsolved hard problem that Qoro is not attempting to solve, positioning the company as an access layer rather than a technical breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Unusual candor for a startup; it narrows the technical risk investors underwrite but also caps defensibility to integration breadth and developer experience.
insights.quote: It’s a hard problem, of course, and we’re not there to solve it. We’re just here to bring access to the users in a simple way.
insights.locator: But it’s always up to the vendor to provide that layer

insights.claim: Qoro operates only in the batch and near-time feedback-loop regimes and does no low-latency work near the QPU and nothing on quantum error correction, arguing those layers require hardware innovation rather than software.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Draws a clean line between the software-addressable market today and the hardware-gated market later — watch whether hardware vendors eventually absorb the near-time orchestration layer.
insights.quote: these low level, you know, right to the computer, this requires more than software, I would say it requires some hardware innovation to get things right
insights.locator: We’re at the top two, more or less

insights.claim: Enterprise customers in energy and finance are described as stuck because they are deeply integrated with IBM while stitching together libraries from multiple sources with no single environment, which is the specific pain Qoro sells into.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Identifies IBM lock-in plus library fragmentation as the concrete wedge for quantum middleware — a leading indicator that vendor-agnostic tooling demand is real, not theoretical.
insights.quote: We see them get stuck because they’re so integrated with IBM, but they’re using libraries from here and here and here, and they don’t know how to put it all into one environment
insights.locator: This is ready today. We’ve already been working with customers

themes.theme: Divi SDK: circuit generation, serialization and parallelization

insights.claim: Divi is Qoro's open-source Python SDK that ingests optimization parameters — QUBO, HUBO or variational quantum algorithms for material science — and automatically translates them into a collection of quantum circuits.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the entry-point SDK is a distribution play; track Divi adoption as the top-of-funnel metric for Qoro's paid cloud and HPC products.
insights.locator: we start with our software layer called Divi

insights.claim: Circuit serialization is called out as a first-order cost problem: producing 10,000 circuits and getting them over the wire is described as very costly, making generation efficiency itself a differentiator.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Data-movement economics, not qubit counts, are the near-term bottleneck in distributed quantum workflows — the same pattern that made networking and interconnect the choke point in classical AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: oftentimes you can produce 10,000 circuits, but getting them over the wire is very costly, or even producing the circuits themselves is very costly
insights.locator: Then we serialize these circuits

insights.claim: Because parallelized circuits are independent, Qoro claims it can immediately provision 50 nodes for a 10,000-circuit workload and obtain near-linear horizontal scaling.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Frames quantum simulation as an embarrassingly parallel cloud workload — meaning the immediate revenue is classical CPU/GPU compute consumption, not quantum hardware.
insights.quote: we can put 50 nodes in place immediately and get a big horizontal improvement there
insights.locator: And then on the simulation side, we scale because we’re parallelizing 10,000 circuits

insights.claim: Time evolution simulation for material science is identified as a naturally parallelizable workload because every point in time must be checked independently.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Materials/chemistry simulation is the workload most likely to consume large parallel compute budgets first — a concrete demand vector for GPU-backed quantum simulation.
insights.locator: So, for example, time evolution is one that we focus on a lot

insights.claim: Error mitigation itself is parallelizable — specifically the folding layers required for zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) — as are search algorithms that partition a solution space.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Error mitigation increases classical compute demand multiplicatively per quantum job, which quietly expands the classical compute TAM attached to every QPU.
insights.quote: You can parallelize error mitigation, for example, when you need to add folding layers for ZNE
insights.locator: So, for example, time evolution is one that we focus on a lot

insights.claim: Choosing an exploratory optimizer such as Monte Carlo sampling or population-based methods converts a serial QAOA feedback loop into a parallelizable batch, letting variational workloads scale horizontally over high-latency internet-connected machines.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A software-only workaround for the latency problem that most people assume requires co-located quantum-classical hardware — undercuts part of the case for on-premise QPU-HPC tight coupling.
insights.quote: you still get this horizontal scale up instantly
insights.locator: And then when we go for the QAOA, for example, where there’s a feedback loop

themes.theme: Maestro: automated simulator and backend selection

insights.claim: Qoro supports 12 different simulation methods across CPU and GPU — including stabilizer, tensor network, Pauli propagation and MPS — and analyzes each circuit to auto-select the optimal engine rather than asking the user.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Simulator-selection automation is a defensible data asset — the routing heuristics improve with every customer circuit and are hard for a single-simulator vendor to replicate.
insights.quote: We support 12 different simulation methods on CPU and GPU
insights.locator: If we send it on the other hand to the simulation platform

insights.claim: The spread between simulation methods is framed as the difference between instantaneous execution and a three-day GPU MPS job on the same circuit, making engine selection an order-of-magnitude cost lever.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Quantifies why routing is worth paying for: mis-selecting a simulator can turn a free job into three days of GPU spend.
insights.quote: Is it a stabilizer simulation? Is it going to be instantaneous? Or is it going to be a three-day job with a GPU MPS-based simulation?
insights.locator: we put a layer there in place to analyze the circuit again

insights.claim: On the hardware path the orchestrator decides on the fly whether a circuit is too connected for a superconducting machine or has too many gates for a trapped-ion machine, and packs multiple circuits onto one device to use qubits efficiently.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Multi-tenanting circuits onto a single QPU raises effective utilization of scarce quantum hardware — a metric QPU operators will care about as they move to cloud economics.
insights.quote: Is it too connected for a superconducting quantum computer? Is it, you know, too many gates for a trapped ion based quantum computer? And we make these decisions on the fly.
insights.locator: Once we send them to the cloud, we have our orchestrator there

insights.claim: Maestro, Qoro's multi-simulator automatic decision maker, was deployed inside CESGA's CUNQA platform, showing the routing layer can be embedded into a third-party HPC software stack rather than only run in Qoro's cloud.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Portability into someone else's platform is what makes an HPC-center licensing model viable; watch for repeat deployments at other national centers.
insights.locator: And later, what we did was introduce our simulation platform Maestro

themes.theme: Plugging into SLURM rather than replacing it

insights.claim: Qoro explicitly will not replace SLURM or PBS Pro and instead ships its orchestration engine as a SLURM plugin that makes the existing scheduler smarter about quantum resources.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Non-displacement is the fastest path into conservative HPC procurement; any vendor trying to replace SLURM faces a far longer sales cycle.
insights.quote: we’re never gonna replace SLURM, we don’t want to go into that direction
insights.locator: It’s precisely in the plugin layer

insights.claim: The unsolved control problem Qoro claims to own is defining what information a QPU must transmit to a classical scheduler so allocation decisions can be made.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Whoever defines the QPU-to-scheduler telemetry interface effectively sets a de facto standard — a quiet standards-capture opportunity worth tracking.
insights.quote: What information should they be transmitting so we can make decisions? This is something we need to control from Qoro side.
insights.locator: It’s precisely in the plugin layer

insights.claim: Qoro envisions two distinct orchestration layers — one routing jobs from the application into the HPC center, and a second inside the center allocating across available GPUs, CPUs and multiple QPUs for hundreds of thousands of concurrent circuits.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Two-layer orchestration implies two separate product/pricing surfaces; optimal in-center allocation is admitted to be future work, so this is roadmap, not shipped capability.
insights.quote: you may have multiple users with hundreds of thousands of circuits that need to be executed at once. And now you need to be making optimal resource allocations.
insights.locator: This could also be two separate layers

insights.claim: In the CESGA pilot, Qoro connected through a secure channel to roughly 15 compute nodes mimicking a distributed quantum network and dispatched 15,000 to 20,000 circuits, generating the application load remotely from outside the center.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A concrete, citable scale figure for remote distributed quantum orchestration — the benchmark against which competing middleware claims should be measured.
insights.quote: we had 15 compute nodes mimicking a quantum computer, and we were generating the application load outside of the center
insights.locator: Yeah, so CESGA is very much aligned with the mentality of Qoro

insights.claim: The entire CESGA integration took about one day of wiring up the secure channel because the abstraction layers were already in place, which Qoro treats as the real result of the proof of concept.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: One-day integration is the sales metric that matters for HPC centers where quantum integration is normally a multi-month project; it directly compresses deployment cost.
insights.quote: this took us just a day of wiring up the secure channel and once it was ready, everything was in place to start running
insights.locator: And so the results were that we could make this connection

insights.claim: The implied end-state from the CESGA work is that individual users can send jobs to national HPC centers from home and access state-of-the-art simulation on state-of-the-art hardware without purchasing anything, using about 20 lines of code.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: If national HPC quantum capacity becomes remotely rentable per-job, it competes directly with commercial quantum cloud offerings on price.
insights.quote: users can be sending jobs to HPCs from their home and you’d be using you know state-of-the-art simulation techniques on state-of-the-art compute technologies without having to purchase a thing
insights.locator: I think the results were that it’s possible

insights.claim: The primary argument for multiple QPUs in an HPC center today is fallback and resilience rather than application scaling — if the single installed quantum computer goes down, the entire user base sits idle for however long maintenance takes.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Reframes multi-vendor QPU procurement from a speculative future need into an operational uptime requirement — a much easier budget line to defend today.
insights.quote: People should be thinking about more quantum computers in the center because you need fallbacks, you need resilience, you need robustness.
insights.locator: I think it’s absolutely necessary

insights.claim: An IBM quantum network outage the day before the interview took all six of IBM's machines offline for about a day simultaneously, demonstrating that single-vendor redundancy is not real redundancy.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Correlated failure across a single vendor's fleet is the strongest concrete case for multi-vendor quantum procurement — and a reputational risk factor for IBM's cloud quantum franchise.
insights.quote: IBM, the network went down for about a day. And we needed those quantum computers. What do we do? They have six of them and they all went down.
insights.locator: we see this repeatedly, even just yesterday

insights.claim: Qoro concedes that multiple quantum computers are not actually necessary for scaling applications today, with the real driver being user experience, production readiness and go-to-market rather than compute capability.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A distributed-quantum-computing founder disavowing the standard distributed-scaling narrative is a useful reality check on multi-QPU marketing claims from other vendors.
insights.quote: When it comes to scaling applications, correct, I don’t think it’s necessary, but it’s more about the user experience and the production readiness and bringing it to market.
insights.locator: People should be thinking about more quantum computers in the center

insights.claim: The forward case for multi-QPU centers is capacity for cloud-scale user counts: selling quantum cloud access to a thousand users is described as impossible on a single machine.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Ties QPU unit demand to end-user seat counts rather than to qubit-count milestones — a different and more tractable demand model for forecasting hardware orders.
insights.quote: if we want to be selling cloud infrastructure and cloud access to quantum computers, supporting a thousand users, can’t have one quantum computer. Need to have more.
insights.locator: When it comes to scaling applications, correct

insights.claim: The customer cost of downtime is framed at roughly a hundred thousand per day on a project with contractors on the payroll, which is the economic justification offered for redundant quantum hardware.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Puts a dollar figure on quantum downtime that makes redundancy spend arithmetic rather than aspirational — useful ammunition in a procurement pitch.
insights.quote: You can’t let your users sit idle if they’re spending a hundred thousand on a project per day or something.
insights.locator: People should be thinking about more quantum computers in the center

themes.theme: Developer experience and the education funnel

insights.claim: The described entry path for new quantum users — pip install Qiskit, follow the Qiskit QAOA guide, then hand-tune mixers, layer counts and optimizers — is presented as the specific friction point where users start needing an abstraction layer.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Qiskit's own onboarding funnel is where a middleware competitor recruits; university curricula are the leading indicator of which toolchain wins the next cohort.
insights.quote: pip install Qiskit, go to Qiskit guide and look at how to implement QAOA
insights.locator: so what we see is we work with universities

insights.claim: The argued failure mode of the current quantum toolchain is that users repeatedly rebuild working components from scratch and paste code snippets between examples instead of composing proven pieces.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Standard-library consolidation historically precedes ecosystem takeoff in developer markets; whoever owns the reusable quantum primitives owns the platform.
insights.quote: Take the pieces that we know work and build on those instead of rebuilding the pieces that we know work every single time you want to do something new.
insights.locator: This is also a problem we face, is how do we convince people

insights.claim: The stated benchmark for good quantum developer experience is a student being able to compare IBM's quantum computer against a QuEra machine on the same QAOA problem out of the box, treating QAOA and variational algorithms as tools rather than projects.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Easy cross-vendor benchmarking commoditizes QPU vendors and shifts pricing power toward whoever controls the comparison layer.
insights.quote: They should be learning engineering problems not software bottlenecks.
insights.locator: If you just want to know what is the input of QAOA

insights.claim: The widely-cited '150,000 lines of code to 20' claim is described by Qoro's own CTO as marketing and a very low estimate, with the real content being 20 lines of configuration code that trigger an entire generated workflow.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Discount headline abstraction-ratio claims in quantum software marketing; the verifiable substance is configuration-driven workflow generation, not a code-volume miracle.
insights.quote: I would say that’s a very, very low estimate. This is a bit of marketing that we do
insights.locator: I read someplace that someone said that you’re replacing 150,000 lines of code

insights.claim: Qoro maintains almost 40 repositories on GitHub, decomposing the hidden infrastructure into separate packages and services that the end user never sees.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Repo count is a checkable proxy for how much of the stack a 10-person team has actually built — verify against the public GitHub org before underwriting the abstraction claim.
insights.quote: We have, I don’t know, almost 40 repos in our GitHub.
insights.locator: So we’re handling so much of the infrastructure

themes.theme: Company, funding and three-tier commercial model

insights.claim: Qoro Quantum was incorporated in 2024, is dual-incorporated in the United Kingdom and Germany with founders split between Munich and the UK, and had just passed its two-year mark at the time of the interview.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A dual UK/Germany structure positions the company for both European sovereign-HPC procurement and UK quantum funding programs.
insights.quote: So we started the company in 2024. We just passed two year mark this month officially.
insights.locator: Tell me a bit about the company

insights.claim: The founding team comes from classical networking rather than quantum hardware — both founders worked at Cisco, with the CTO researching quantum networks and distributed quantum computing and the co-founder Dan coming from national and data-center network deployment on the business side.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A networking-native founding team explains the routing/orchestration framing and suggests the company will be evaluated on interconnect logic, not physics.
insights.quote: I worked at Cisco as well as Dan, and I was researching quantum network technologies
insights.locator: And we come from a background of network technologies

insights.claim: Qoro is roughly 10 full-time employees, raised a pre-seed in March and expects to close a seed round by the end of summer.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Very early stage with an imminent seed — the CESGA proof point and the IBM-outage narrative are almost certainly the raise story; expect the round to be announced shortly after publication.
insights.quote: We just raised a pre-seed in March and we’re looking into finishing a seed round coming hopefully by the end of summer.
insights.locator: The team now is 10 full time

insights.claim: The self-serve product is a pay-as-you-go credit system with an API token, no contracts, and immediate cloud access to CPUs and GPUs for Divi-built applications.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A contract-free credit funnel in enterprise quantum is unusual and gives a cheap read on genuine bottom-up developer demand versus grant-funded pilots.
insights.quote: get an API token and start running immediately with no contracts, it’s pay as you go
insights.locator: So our products are threefold in a sense

insights.claim: The HPC offering is an open-core model — much of the software is open source with premium features sold as a service — alongside dedicated infrastructure-as-a-service with reserved compute nodes for enterprise research teams.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Open-core plus dedicated IaaS is the standard path to HPC-center budgets; margin depends entirely on how much value sits above the open-source line.
insights.quote: it’s an open core type model with premium features as a service
insights.locator: And so with an HPC center, we have two different things

insights.claim: Qoro sells HPC centers an emulation-based integration demo that reproduces the full quantum software stack and control technologies without a physical QPU, pitched as spending 100k-200k instead of one to five million to learn what owning a quantum computer feels like.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: A 10x-cheaper substitute for a QPU purchase could delay or displace real hardware orders at budget-constrained centers — a genuine demand risk for quantum hardware vendors.
insights.quote: if they need to invest a million or five million just to see how it feels to have a quantum computer, it’s a lot more risky if they can spend, let’s say, 100k or 200k to see the same thing
insights.locator: And then the second is an integration demo

insights.claim: The interviewer Yuval Boger is the Chief Commercial Officer of QuEra Computing, meaning this vendor-agnostic middleware pitch is being examined by an executive at a competing quantum hardware company.
insights.speaker: Quantum Computing Report
insights.so_what: Read the hardware-side pushback in this interview — 'to what extent are you ahead of your time' — as a signal of how QPU vendors themselves assess middleware timing.
insights.locator: Yuval Boger is the Chief Commercial Officer
